opener.heading: Week 16: Earth Day & Wildlife 🌎
about: Seven days of working out who else lives on this street. Azlyn tallies what goes past the window and tapes the animals back onto the glass, measures a tree with a length of string, tests which coat a duck would wear, dams a roasting pan until it bursts, tears every newspaper in the house into a grassland deep enough to lie in, and colors twelve lizards to vanish on twelve surfaces. One question sits under all of it: what lives here, and what does it need to stay?

Earth Day is Thursday, Day 112, and it takes the whole day. The morning is one stretch of sidewalk and one bag, photographed from the same spot before and after, with the number of pieces counted out loud as they drop in. The afternoon gives a corner of the garden away and leaves it alone until Christmas. Three things outlast the week: the tree string, dated and taped up the wall beside the growth chart, the paper animals in their soap tree at the window, and the wild corner with her name on a craft stick in front of it.
azlyn: Tallying. One crayon mark per animal in one of four boxes, a good stretch at the glass, then every box counted out loud with a finger on each mark.
Measuring with string. A length round the tree trunk, then one for the sofa, the door, Kreston lying down and her own middle, taped up the wall and read shortest to longest.
Committing to a number. She says how many pitchers the dam holds before the first pour, watches it go at two, and gives you a different number for the rebuild.
Matching a color to a surface. Twelve lizards colored against the sofa arm, the fridge door and the curtain, each one held up to the thing to check before she cuts it out.
Hand work, in bursts all week. Tearing newspaper down the grain, cutting animals out with child-safe scissors, rubbing bark through paper, working a pair of kitchen tongs.
you: Looking out a window counts as an activity
Recovery days are the right time to start something slow
The transition seasons are the hardest, and the weather is only part of it
Predicting the breaking point is real experimental thinking
Destruction before construction is a legitimate sequence
"What could we change?" is the most useful question in this book
Leaving and coming back is its own lesson

days.title: Who Else Lives Here
days.prepTonight: Clear the sill of whichever window has the most street in it, and leave the paper, a thick marker, the crayons and the masking tape on it.

schedule.label: Quiet Play
schedule.name: The Animals Left on the Windowsill

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: The Book with the Big Animals In It

opening.title: The Watching Seat
steps: Carry the chair round the downstairs and let her pick the window.
Cushion on the seat, blanket over the back. She builds it, you hold the chair still while she climbs on.
Sit with her for five minutes and name every living thing that goes past. Get down before she is bored, and tell her the counting starts at 9:15.

main.title: The Tally at the Glass
materials: The chair at the window, with its cushion and blanket
steps: Fold the paper in half twice and open it flat for four boxes. In marker, draw a bird, a dog, a cat and a fat question mark, one to a box.
Tape it to the glass low enough that she can reach the bottom of every box.
Sit in the seat together. Every time something alive goes past she puts a crayon mark in its box, and the mark stands even when it lands in the wrong one.
The question mark is the good box: a squirrel, a crow, something that moved in the hedge. She decides what counts.
When she has had enough, or at twenty minutes, count the marks in each box out loud, touching every one. Ask her which box won.
Leave the sheet taped to the glass. She works off it at 1:00.
main.tip: The first few minutes are empty and she will want to get down. Keep a crayon in your own hand and mark the first one yourself. She takes the job back the second something moves.

outside.title: The Two-Minute Stand
paras: Walk to the nearest hedge, wall or scrap of rough grass and stand still for two full minutes. No talking. Time it on your phone where she can watch the numbers run out. April is the loudest month out there, every bird singing over every other since dawn. Let her tell you what she heard, then stand again on the way home and see whether she names the same things.

days.infant: Kreston is 10 months and points at things to show you, which is new. Hold him at the glass while Azlyn marks her sheet and name whatever his finger lands on, even when it is a parked car. Take him out of the stroller for the two-minute stand and hold him facing the hedge. He goes still when you do.

second.title: The Animals on the Glass
second.intro: The animals come off the tally sheet and get a tree to sit in, drawn onto the window with a wet bar of soap.
steps: Read the tally back. Every mark is one animal, so she draws one of each: the birds, the dog, the cat, and whatever went in the question-mark box.
She colors them in, hand-sized or wider, because small ones tear the moment she cuts them.
She cuts them out with the child-safe scissors. Rough edges are fine.
Dip the soap in the bowl of water and draw a tree onto the glass: you do the trunk, she does the branches. Soap dries white and lifts off with the damp cloth.
Tape the animals into the tree facing out at the street. She decides who sits high and who goes on the ground.
Stand on the path outside and look back at the window, then come in and look out through it. Leave it up.
second.tip: Soap comes off with the damp cloth, so let her draw as much of the window as she wants.

alternatives: Draw the animals onto the glass with soap and skip the paper.
Sort the cut-outs into who flies and who walks.
Tape them round the bathroom mirror instead.
One animal each, drawn huge, and stop there.
outAgain: A friend's house, and take four paper animals to give away
The park, to look for the real versions of what is on your window
A slow lap of the block with the tally sheet
The garden center, for the pond and whatever lives in it
A café with a window seat, and count what goes past

aroundWorld.title: Kenya, Wangari Maathai 🌳
paras: Wangari Maathai grew up in Kenya beside a stream and a fig tree her mother told her never to cut. Years later, with the hills around her stripped bare, she paid women a few shillings for every seedling they raised. The Green Belt Movement she built has put more than fifty million trees in the ground across Kenya.
aroundWorld.tryIt: Cook sukuma wiki, the greens Kenyan families eat most nights. Shred kale or collard greens, fry them with onion and tomato, and eat it with rice. Azlyn strips the leaves off the stalks.
aroundWorld.didYouKnow: She was the first African woman to win the Nobel Peace Prize.

days.krestonPM: Give him a whole sheet of paper on the floor and a fat crayon. At 10 months he holds it in his fist and bangs more than he draws, and the mark surprises him. Keep the cut-outs and the scissors up on the table while he is down there. He cruises the furniture now, and the windowsill is at his height.

insight.headline: Looking out a window counts as an activity.
paras: Azlyn sat looking at a street this morning, ten minutes on a bad day and twenty on a good one. The marks are the smallest part of it. Sustained attention on one slow thing is the skill school will ask for, and almost nothing else in her day builds it. A window gives her a frame, a slow rate of change and no requirement to produce anything. Attention stretches on a slow task and shortens on a fast one, which is worth knowing on a morning with nothing quick in it. The days you park her at the glass because you are holding Kreston and cannot do anything else are doing more work than they feel like doing.

days.safety: Blind and curtain cords are a strangulation risk and the chair puts both children in reach of them. Tie every cord up out of reach or cleat it to the wall before she climbs on. Nothing gets stacked under the window: Kreston pulls to stand on whatever is there, and the chair is not a step. Child-safe scissors only, and they go back in the drawer when she stops cutting. Soap water stays in the bowl and off her face, and the floor under the window gets the damp cloth so nobody slips.

days.title: Our Tree
days.prepTonight: Peel the paper off four wax crayons and pack the string, scissors, paper, marker and masking tape into a bag by the door.

schedule.label: Her Job

schedule.label: Wind-Down

opening.title: The Crayon on Its Side
opening.need: 2 sheets of paper · 2 peeled wax crayons · 1 coin.
steps: Lay a sheet over the coin and rub the flat of the crayon across it. The coin comes up out of the paper.
Send her round the room for three more things to rub: floorboards, radiator, the sole of her shoe.
Tell her the last rubbing today comes off a tree.

main.title: The Tree with Her String On It
materials: 4 wax crayons with the paper peeled off
1 bag to carry it all in
steps: Walk until she picks a tree, even when it is the scruffy one by the trash cans. Whichever one she stops at is the one, and you measure that one.

Pick a landmark on the trunk at her shoulder height: a fork, a knot, the top of the ivy. Say it out loud so you both have it. Wrap the string round the trunk at that mark, bring the ends together and cut.
Write the date and the landmark on a strip of tape in permanent marker, wrap it round one end of the string, and fold the string into the bag.
Tape a sheet of paper to the bark and rub a crayon flat across it until the pattern comes through. Do a second where the bark changes.
Name the tree. Whatever she says is the name, and you use it from now on.
Photograph her with both arms round the trunk, and let her decide how far round she can reach before you take it.
main.tip: A trunk is narrower the higher you go, so the landmark you both said out loud matters more than the height of her shoulder. Write it on the flag in the words she used and the string means something a year from now.

outside.title: Ten Minutes Looking Up
paras: Lie down under the tree with her, heads together, and look up through it for ten minutes. Mid-April is the week the leaves arrive: some branches bare, some half open, the sunny side ahead of the rest. Count the birds that cross the gap. Take something to lie on, because the ground is still cold.

days.infant: Kreston is 10 months and pulls up on furniture, so give him the trunk. He holds it the way he holds the sofa, and bark under his palms is a texture nothing indoors gives him. Lay him on his back beside Azlyn for the ten minutes of looking up. He tracks the branches longer than she does.

second.title: The House in String
second.intro: The tree's length goes up the wall beside the growth chart, and everything else in the house gets a string beside it.
materials: The tree string from this morning
The growth chart wall from Day 1
steps: Tape the tree string flat up the wall beside the growth chart, one end on the floor. She will want to stand against it.
Ask her what to measure next and take her list in her order: the sofa, the door, Kreston lying down, her own middle.
Cut a length for each. She holds one end, you cut. Write what it is on a tape flag and stick it at the top.
Tape every string flat up the wall side by side, all starting on the floor, nothing hanging and no loops.
Read the wall with her, shortest to longest, then let her reorder them and leave whatever she lands on.
Measure yourself last and let her mark on your string where hers reaches.
Leave the tree string up on the wall. It is the one thing going up there that is not going to change, and everything beside it will.
second.tip: Cut each string a hand longer than the thing you measured. She pulls them off the wall to hold two side by side, and one cut to length loses a centimeter going back up.

alternatives: One string for her, one for the tree, and stop there.
Measure the same things in hand-spans.
Lay the strings along the hall floor instead.
Cut a string for everyone in the house.
outAgain: The botanical garden, and find the widest trunk in it
The park, with the string, to see whether a tree there matches
The garden center, to look at trees small enough to carry
The woods loop, and name a second tree
A café, if the rain wins
days.krestonPM: He goes on the wall too. Lay him at the baseboard, run the string from his heel to his head and cut. At 10 months he will not hold still, so take the longest of three tries. Put the string away and give him the empty bag, because he posts a hand into anything with a mouth to it.

insight.headline: Recovery days are the right time to start something slow.
paras: Saturday after a full week is when you have the least left, and it is the right day to start a thing that takes a year. Measuring a tree costs nine minutes and returns nothing today, and it goes up on the wall anyway, where she will walk past it for months. Slow work survives because it asks almost nothing on any single day: one string, one date, one photograph. The string sits beside her own pencil marks, and the two make the same point from opposite directions. Hers moves up the frame. The tree's stays where she put it. Azlyn cannot hold a year in her head at three, so the wall holds it for her.

days.safety: Cut string is a strangulation risk and Kreston is 10 months and pulling up on everything. Tape each string flat to the wall along its whole length so there is nothing hanging and no loop. Offcuts go back in the bag as you make them, never on the floor. The scissors stay with you. The coin goes back in your pocket the moment she finishes the first rubbing, because Kreston is 10 months, picks up single small things between finger and thumb, and a coin is the size he chokes on.

days.title: Staying Dry
days.prepTonight: Dig out three layers with different surfaces (a waterproof, a wool sweater, a cotton shirt) and leave them on the sofa with a teaspoon and a cup.

schedule.label: Opening Activity
schedule.name: Three Coats and a Drop of Water

schedule.label: Get Outside
schedule.name: Shaking It Off at the Pond

schedule.label: Her Job
schedule.name: The Boots Lined Up by the Door

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: A Hot Bath and Dry Pajamas

opening.title: Three Coats and a Drop of Water
opening.need: 3 layers (waterproof, wool, cotton) · 1 teaspoon · 1 cup of water.
steps: Lay the three on the floor and let her run a hand over each first.
Drip a teaspoon of water onto each in turn. She watches the drop sit, soak in or roll off.
Ask which she would wear out in the rain. Take her answer, tell her a duck has the same problem, and leave it until 9:15.

main.title: The Duck That Stays Dry
materials: Wax crayons, one of them thick
Food coloring, 2 drops (optional, makes the water visible)
steps: Draw a duck on each sheet, the same size, both of them hers to color.
She fills one in solid with wax crayon, every scrap of white covered, pressing hard and going over it twice. That is the duck with oil on its feathers. The second stays plain.
Lay both on the tray and stir two drops of food coloring into the cup.
Ask her which duck soaks through first. Take her call before a drop lands.
Drip a teaspoon onto each duck's back. The wax duck holds the water in beads on top. The plain one goes dark, soft and see-through.
Hold both up to the window. Dry the tray with the dish towel and run it again with a whole spoonful on each.
main.tip: Send her back over the gaps before you pour.

outside.title: Shaking It Off at the Pond
paras: Stand at the pond and wait for a duck to climb out. Water runs off its back in beads and the bird walks away dry, which is this morning's crayon duck in real feathers. Watch one shake itself: head first, then the body, then the tail, and the whole thing is over in a second. Count the shakes before you turn for home. On the way back, run her hand down a wet fence rail and then down the sleeve of her coat, and ask which one kept the water.

days.infant: Kreston is 10 months and understands "no", which he shows by stopping, looking at you, and doing it again to check. Give him water of his own: strap him into the high chair and put 1 shallow unbreakable dish with a splash of water on his tray. He slaps it flat-handed and watches what comes back up at him. Outside he points at the ducks and you name them.

second.title: Eight Ways Across the Room
second.intro: Each card names the animal she has to be to cross the room.
materials: A cleared stretch of floor, the longest in the house
steps: Draw one animal on each card: frog, snake, bear, flamingo, crab, elephant, rabbit, penguin. Rough drawings. She names each as it appears under the marker.
Lay all eight face down at one end of the cleared floor.
She turns one over and you both cross the room that way. Frogs jump, snakes go on their bellies, bears walk on hands and feet, flamingos stand on one leg the whole distance.
Once she has the idea, put the cushions down as rocks halfway across so every animal has to get over something.
The scarf goes down as a river for the last stretch. Snakes go through it, flamingos step over, crabs go round.
Let her invent two of her own and draw them on the backs of two cards.
Finish on the slowest animal either of you can think of and cross the room in silence.
second.tip: A bear crawl she does on her own lasts four seconds. A bear crawl with you alongside lasts the length of the room.

alternatives: Four cards instead of eight, and skip the cushions.
Move like the animals taped to the window on Friday.
One crossing under a blanket, one way only.
Put the cards in a bag and pull them out blind.
outAgain: A playground you have never been to, picked off the map on the way there
The duck pond, in whatever the sky is doing
A puddle walk in rain boots with no other plan attached
The woods, to see how much greener they went this week
A drive and a stop for fries, if the rain sets in
days.krestonPM: Put him on the cleared floor with you both. At 10 months he cruises the furniture and drops to his hands to move fast. Crawl the bear crossing beside him and let him chase Azlyn down the room. Keep the cards in your hand and the scarf over your shoulder while he is down there, and turn each card where he cannot reach it.

insight.headline: The transition seasons are the hardest, and the weather is only part of it.
paras: April will not commit. You dress both children for cold and it turns warm by ten, or you plan a day outdoors and the sky opens at half past nine. Azlyn builds her sense of what happens next out of what the day looks like, and a spring where the same hour is bright on Monday and streaming on Tuesday hands her nothing to predict from, so she asks you the same question all morning. Keep one thing fixed that the weather cannot touch: the same seat, the same walk, the same order to the day. She borrows her steadiness off that.

days.safety: Kreston gets his own dish on the high chair tray, and no standing water sits within his reach. The duck tray goes up on the counter the moment you finish with it. Food coloring stains skin, grout and clothes and belongs nowhere near a mouth, so the cup and the tray stay on your side of the table. The scarf and the eight cards come up off the floor whenever he is loose down there, because a scarf across the route of a cruising baby puts him over, and card corners come back chewed. Hold on to both of them at the pond, because a bank you can stand on is a bank you can go off.

days.title: The Dam
days.prepTonight: Stand the roasting pan, two old towels, a wooden spoon and the pitcher by the back door, with the playdough out of the fridge if there is no garden.

schedule.label: Her Job
schedule.name: The Towels to the Washing Machine

opening.title: The Tilted Tray
opening.need: the roasting pan · 1 wooden spoon · 1 pitcher of water · 2 old towels.
steps: Lay both towels down, stand the pan on them, and prop one end on the wooden spoon.
Let her pour a little water in at the high end and watch it pool at the bottom.
Pull the spoon out so the pan sits flat and pour again. Ask where the water goes now, and leave the question until 9:15.

main.title: The Dam That Holds
materials: 1 roasting pan, dishpan or under-bed storage box
A fistful of soil or mud (playdough if there is no garden)
1 wooden spoon to prop the tray at a slope
steps: Prop the tray on the wooden spoon with both towels underneath, high end away from her.
Send her out twice for the sticks and stones. Whatever she brings back is the whole supply.
Build across the middle: a line of stones first, sticks laid against them, mud pressed into every gap. Her hands do the mud.
Ask how many pitchers it holds before it breaks. Take her number and say it back.
Pour one pitcher in at the high end. Stop. Look. Pour the next. Count them off as they go.
It breaks. Look at where it went first, rebuild that end and nothing else, and pour again.
main.tip: Mud is the part she will skip. Stones and sticks alone let the water straight through, so make her press mud into every gap before the first pour.

outside.title: Following the Water Downhill
paras: Go out after the rain and find water on the move: the gutter along the curb, a drain, a rut worn into a footpath. Walk beside it until it drops out of sight down a grate. Let her block it with the side of her boot and watch the puddle build behind her foot. Rain boots on, and two wet sleeves come home.

days.infant: Kreston is 10 months, fast and low, and this is the one activity you keep him out of. Sit him in the high chair beside you with an empty bowl and a spoon and let him bang while Azlyn pours. On the walk, stop the stroller at every drain so he can hear it. He turns his whole head toward running water and holds still.

second.title: Bursting It on Purpose
second.intro: She builds the dam again and breaks it on purpose, with a cork floating above it to show what the water carries off.
materials: The tray, propped on the wooden spoon
All the dam materials: sticks, stones, mud
1 cork, or a small plastic animal
Chalk or masking tape, to mark the water line
steps: Rebuild the dam on the propped tray, towels underneath. Kreston goes in the high chair beside you for the whole ninety minutes, and he stays in it if you move the tray to the bath instead. She builds this one and you hand her pieces as she asks.
Fill behind it a pitcher at a time. Let the water settle, then mark the line it reaches with chalk or tape.
Float the cork on the water above the dam.
Let her pull one single piece out of the dam. She picks which. Both of you watch the cork.
Empty the tray into the bucket and pour it on a houseplant or the grass.
Now she builds one she thinks survives four pitchers. Mark that prediction next to the first line.
Pour four pitchers. She is right or she is wrong, and the last pour is hers either way.
second.tip: Two chalk marks an inch apart tell her which dam was better quicker than the water does.

alternatives: The same dam built in the bath.
A dam in the sink with the plug out.
Dig a channel in the mud outside and pour a pitcher down it.
Sort the stones by size and stop there.
outAgain: A hill walk, and look for where the water runs off the top
The riverside path, to find a real weir and stand above it
The neighborhood park, if the legs have gone
The woods loop, wet underfoot and worth it
The duck pond, and stand where the water comes in
days.krestonPM: The tray goes up on the table the moment you finish and the bucket goes outside. Put him down on a dry towel with an empty plastic pitcher. At 10 months he tips, drops and turns things over to find the far side, and a pitcher gives him that without a drop of water in the room.

insight.headline: Predicting the breaking point is real experimental thinking.
paras: Azlyn said four pitchers and it went at two. On the rebuild she said two and got five. The number is what separates this from watching water. A quantity commits her to something checkable, and she has to revise it in front of you when the tray proves her wrong. That revision is the piece that carries: she holds a rule about mud and gaps, tests it, changes it. Take her number at face value and hold her to it out loud. Being wrong costs a three-year-old nothing, and softening it removes the only reason the second pour is interesting.

days.safety: Standing water and a 10-month-old who cruises. Water that shallow is enough to drown in, so the tray goes up on the table or gets emptied into the bucket the second you step away, and it never sits on the floor while he is loose. Small stones are a choking size. Count them back into the bucket and sweep before he goes down.

days.title: Grassland on the Floor
days.prepTonight: Stop the recycling going out. Pile every newspaper, catalog and junk-mail envelope into a box by the sofa, with a bedsheet and a trash bag beside it.

schedule.name: The Uncut Bit by the Fence

schedule.label: Her Job
schedule.name: Scraping the Plates into the Caddy

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: The Last Half Hour in the Grass

opening.title: Here or Far Away
opening.need: 8–10 animal pictures (a book, a magazine, Friday's cut-outs) · 2 sheets of paper · 1 marker.
steps: Write HERE on one sheet and FAR AWAY on the other, a meter apart on the floor.
Go through the animals and let her put each on a sheet. Pigeon here, lion far away, and the fox starts an argument.
Count the far-away pile. Ask what the ground looks like where those ones live, and tell her you are building it at 9:15.

main.title: The Long Grass
materials: A stack of newspaper and junk mail, everything in the house
1 large cardboard box or laundry basket to hold it
1 trash bag for the end of the day
steps: Spread the bedsheet on the floor. Everything happens on it, so the room clears in one lift tonight.
Show her the tear: hold the top of a newspaper page in both hands and pull down the grain. It runs straight and it is loud.
Tear until the box is full, then keep going. Grass deep enough to lie in takes more than you think, so tear alongside her and expect to be the one who finishes it.
Tape three or four long strips together at one end for tall clumps, and stand them against the sofa.
Tip the box out over the sheet and let her spread it until it covers a stretch she can lie in.
Lie down in it together and stay quiet for a minute. Ask what might be in here that neither of you can see.
main.tip: Newspaper tears straight one way and shreds the other. Hand her the page turned the right way and she finds the grain herself.

outside.title: The Uncut Bit by the Fence
paras: Find the patch nobody mows: the strip along a fence, the edge of a parking lot, the corner behind the trash cans. Late April is when it takes off, and grass that lay flat in March is at her knee. Kneel and part it with your hands. Everything lives in the bottom four inches: beetles, a snail on a stem, the flattened runs where something pushed through.

days.infant: Kreston is 10 months and paper goes in his mouth before it goes anywhere else. Give him one whole broadsheet page, too big to get into his mouth, and let him crumple it. The noise is the draw, and he works at it a few minutes at a time and comes back to it three or four times across the hour. Keep him off the torn pile, because strips are the wrong size. Outside, hold him low enough to reach the grass.

second.title: The Waterhole on the Floor
second.intro: A blue towel goes down in a clearing as the only water for miles, and every animal in the house comes to it.
materials: The toy animals, every one you can find
steps: Clear a space in the middle of the grass and lay the blue towel in it. That is the water. Kreston watches from the high chair beside you for the whole ninety minutes.
The cushions go down at one end as rocks. The shoebox goes on its side as shelter, taped at the corners so it holds shape.
Bring every animal in the house to the edge of the grass. She decides who lives here, and the rest go back in their box.
Play it through. Morning at the waterhole, everyone comes down to drink. Take whichever animal she hands you.
Turn the big light off, give her the flashlight, and run it again at night. Different animals come out and she tells you which.
Hide one animal in the shelter and let the rest hunt through the grass for it.
Leave it standing. She goes back into it on her own at 4:15.
second.tip: Play the part she gives you the way she tells you. The plot is hers, and the moment you start improving it she hands you a smaller part.

alternatives: Blue towel on bare floor, no grass, same animals.
Sort the animals into who drinks and who hunts.
Build one hide out of two cushions and a sheet.
Take the flashlight and the animals under the dining table.
outAgain: Swimming
The park, if the session is canceled
Indoor playground, if it is streaming down
The duck pond, and count who comes to the water
A field walk, for grass she can lose herself in
days.krestonPM: He swims too. At 10 months he cruises furniture, so hold both his hands and let him walk the shallow ledge along the poolside the way he walks the sofa. Twenty minutes, then out and warm. Back home he stays on your hip or in the high chair while the grass is down, and the torn paper goes in the bag after her wind-down.

insight.headline: Destruction before construction is a legitimate sequence.
paras: Azlyn tore paper in bursts all morning and nothing existed at the end of it except a pile. Tearing is a two-handed job that builds the grip she will hold a pencil with, and it hands her an outcome she controls outright: pull, and it comes apart. Taking something to pieces first also settles her for the building that comes after, which is why this order beats the other one. The wreckage is also the material. A morning that leaves nothing standing is easy to write off, and this one paid for the afternoon. She destroyed the newspapers and then lay down in a grassland.

days.safety: Torn paper and small plastic animals are both a choking size for Kreston at 10 months. He gets his own whole page and nothing smaller than his fist. Sweep and bag the strips before he goes down, and count the animals back into their box. Swimming this afternoon. Both children stay within arm's reach in the water at all times, and no float or seat is a substitute for your hands.

days.title: The Ones You Can't See
days.prepTonight: Flatten the biggest cardboard box you have and stand it behind the sofa, with the green and brown paper and the masking tape on the table.

schedule.label: Her Job
schedule.name: Carrying the Plates to the Table

schedule.label: Quiet Play
schedule.name: Behind the Hide on Her Own

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: Bath, Then the Hide by Flashlight

opening.title: Three Things That Match
opening.need: the crayon box · 1 pencil · 1 sheet of paper.
steps: She picks three crayons out of the box. Any three, and no steering.
Walk the house and find one thing that matches each: the sofa arm, a floor tile, the fridge door. She holds the crayon against it to check.
Write the three matches on the sheet in pencil. Tell her the lizards get made at 9:15 and have to disappear on those.

main.title: The Lizards That Vanish
materials: 6 sheets of paper or thin card
steps: Draw twelve lizards in pencil, two to a sheet, hand-length with a fat tail. She draws as many as she wants and you do the rest.
Walk the house and pick twelve surfaces: the sofa arm, a bathroom tile, the wooden floor, the fridge door, the curtain, a bookshelf.
She colors one lizard per surface, holding the paper against the thing to check the match.
She cuts all twelve out with the child-safe scissors.
She hides them while you shut your eyes and count to twenty. A loop of tape holds the ones that need a wall.
Hunt them one at a time. Finding eleven and giving up on the last is the normal ending. Swap over and let her hunt yours.
main.tip: The lizard she colors against the patterned curtain is the one you will not find. Let her take the hard surfaces.

outside.title: Green on Green
paras: Take the two greenest lizards out and hold them against things until you find one they disappear on. Late April offers new grass, ivy on a wall, the underside of a fresh leaf. Then look for the real ones: a green stink bug on a stem, a caterpillar the color of its leaf, a moth flat on bark. Stand still and give your eyes a minute.

days.infant: Kreston is 10 months and points at what he wants you to look at, which makes him useful in a hunt. Carry him round the room while Azlyn hides, then watch where his finger goes. He picks out high-contrast shapes on a plain wall before she does. Give him one lizard on a whole sheet, and take it back before it comes apart.

second.title: The Hide by the Window
second.intro: A cardboard screen with a hole cut in it goes up at the window, and she watches the street without the street watching her.
materials: 1 craft knife or heavy scissors (adult only)
Green and brown paper, or real leaves and grass
The chair from Friday's watching seat
steps: Stand the box up at a second window, leaving Friday's soap tree and its animals on their own glass. Hold the box while she sits behind, so you can mark the peephole at her eye height.
Cut the peephole yourself, a hand-sized square, and score the side panels so they fold forward and it stands. The knife goes out of reach the moment you finish.
She covers the street side: green and brown paper taped on in overlapping strips, leaves and grass under the tape, crayon over the bare patches.
Tape the folded edges to the chair legs so it cannot topple forward.
Cushion behind it. She gets in with the fresh tally sheet and a crayon.
Sit outside the hide and be the one who cannot see her. Ask what is out there.
Leave it standing. She goes back behind it at 4:15 and after her bath.
second.tip: Cut the peephole small. A big hole turns it into a window, and a hide works by seeing out further than anyone sees in.

alternatives: A blanket over the sofa back with one gap to look through.
Cover the screen in yesterday's newspaper grass.
Cut two peepholes so both of you fit behind it.
Draw the street from behind the hide instead of tallying.
outAgain: Indoor playground, the quiet session
The park, and five minutes still on a bench before you move
The woods loop, to see what hides in the new leaves
The library, if you would both rather be still
A café with a window seat, watched the way she watched the street
days.krestonPM: The hide is a wall at his height and he will pull up on it, so tape it to the chair legs before he goes down near it. Give him a spare flap of cardboard laid flat, with a strip of green paper taped to it. At 10 months he lifts a single strip with finger and thumb and works one edge a long time.

insight.headline: "What could we change?" is the most useful question in this book.
paras: You have been asking it since January and it has done more work than any activity in here. The question hands the problem back without handing over the answer. It assumes something can be changed, which is the part Azlyn cannot supply for herself at three, and it leaves the choice of what to change open to her. Set it against "the green one doesn't work, try brown", which fixes this lizard and teaches her nothing about the next. Ask it over a dam, a tower, a hiding place, a coat zip that has stuck. Say it flat, with your hands off the thing, and leave the pause after it long enough to feel rude.

days.safety: The craft knife is adult only. It goes back out of reach between cuts, on a shelf and not on the windowsill. Tape the standing screen to the chair legs or lay it flat, because Kreston pulls up on anything at his height and cardboard will come down on him. Paper offcuts off the floor before he goes down. Azlyn's are the child-safe pair, back in the drawer when she stops.

days.title: Leave It Better
days.prepTonight: Tomorrow is Earth Day. Find the kitchen tongs, dig out gloves for both of you, and leave two grocery bags, the soap and a towel by the front door.

schedule.label: Get Outside
schedule.name: The Bench and the Three Things

schedule.label: Quiet Play
schedule.name: The Tongs and the Bowl of Pasta

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: Bath and the Photographs from Today

opening.title: Picking It Up Without Hands
opening.need: 1 pair of kitchen tongs · 1 bowl · 10 things off the floor.
steps: Scatter ten things across the floor (a sock, a crayon, a toy car, a leaf) with the bowl in the middle.
She picks every one up with the tongs and drops it in the bowl. No hands. Tongs are hard at three.
Once she can work them, tell her what they are for at 9:15, and that nothing goes in her hands.

main.title: One Street, One Bag
materials: Rubber or gardening gloves, 1 pair each
Your phone, for the before and the after
Hand soap and a towel by the door
steps: Pick one stretch and name it out loud: the wall to the mailbox, the bus stop to the gate. Fifty meters is plenty.
Stand at one end and photograph it. Let her take the picture and let it be crooked.
Gloves on both of you. She works the tongs, you hold the bag open. Anything sharp, any glass, any can, anything neither of you can name, you pick up.
Count out loud as each piece drops in, and say the running number back every ten.
Photograph the same stretch from the same spot and tell her the final number.
Bag straight in the bin. Gloves off, then both of you at the sink with soap and the towel.
main.tip: Twenty minutes on one stretch she can see the end of gives her a finished thing to stand in.

outside.title: The Bench and the Three Things
paras: Sit on a bench with a long view and find three things nobody made: a tree, a cloud, moss in the mortar. Then three that somebody did. She will argue about the grass coming up through the sidewalk. Late April gives you birdsong from every direction, so stop talking and count how many you hear.

days.infant: Kreston is 10 months and understands "no". He stays strapped in the stroller for the litter pick, with the bag on the far handle. Give him measuring spoons on a ring. On the bench, sit him on your knee facing the road: he points at every bird that crosses and waits for you to name it.

second.title: The Wild Corner
second.intro: You give one corner of the garden back and leave it alone until Christmas.
materials: Sticks and fallen branches, an armful
1 flat stone or a broken tile, plus 1 smaller stone to prop it
1 old plant pot or a chipped mug
1 craft stick and 1 marker, for the name label
1 bucket to carry it all in
steps: Walk the garden and let her choose the corner, somewhere nobody walks and nothing gets mown.
Fill the bucket with sticks and pile them loose, because a tight pile has nowhere to live in it.
Heap the dead leaves against the stick pile and leave them.
Lay the flat stone at the edge, one side propped on the smaller stone so there is a gap under it. Things move in under stones inside two weeks.
Lay the plant pot on its side in the leaves, half buried, mouth out.
Push two sticks in at the front corners and run the string between them. That is the boundary, and it tells the house to leave it alone.
Write her chosen name on the craft stick, push it in beside the string, and photograph the lot.
second.tip: Choose the corner you can see from a window. One behind the shed is forgotten by June.

alternatives: A stick pile in a big pot on the balcony.
Sort today's litter into what could have been recycled.
Draw the wild corner and what she thinks moves in first.
Stuff a plant pot with hollow stalks and hang it on a fence.
outAgain: The pharmacy and then the park bench, and let her hand the slip over
The park, picking up three pieces on the way out
A walk to the recycling bins with whatever is in the box
The garden center, for something that feeds bees
The duck pond, and a look along the bank
days.krestonPM: Put him on a blanket at the edge of the garden with two of the longest sticks, far too long to get near his mouth, and let him bang them together. At 10 months he cruises, so give him something solid at his height: a low wall, a garden chair, your leg.

insight.headline: Leaving and coming back is its own lesson.
paras: The wild corner does nothing today. Azlyn piled sticks into it and walked away, and everything worth having sits three months out. Children under four hold almost no sense of a season, and they build one by returning to the same spot and finding it changed. Photograph the corner and date the picture, then take her back to it on any morning you think of it, with the picture in her hand. She will not remember the corner. She will recognize it, which is a different thing and enough at three, and she finds the difference herself. Her own pencil marks on the door frame work the same way, and she checks those without being asked.

days.safety: Litter picking means broken glass, cans, dog mess and needles. Tongs and gloves only, never bare hands, and you pick up anything sharp while she stands back. The bag stays on your side and away from Kreston. If you find a needle, leave it and call the city. Wash the tongs in hot soapy water before they go back in the kitchen drawer, and wash both pairs of hands with soap before anyone eats. Run the boundary string low and taut between two short sticks with nothing hanging off it, and keep Kreston's blanket at the far end of the garden from it.
